title: Institutional limits on a unitary executive
shortTitle: Institutional limits on a unitary executive
summary: Statutes, appropriations, Senate confirmation, federalism, private enforcement, and contracting distribute implementation across institutions the President cannot fully direct.
notes:
The unitary-executive debate asks whether the Constitution grants the President policy control over every executive administrator’s discretion. The assigned conclusion separately considers practical capacity: even a broad legal theory must contend with a large, internally differentiated executive branch. Saikrishna Prakash identifies Congress’s creation and funding of offices, statutory limits on discretion, and Senate participation in appointments as structural constraints. Coordination bodies and personnel screening respond to some of those constraints without eliminating them.

Citizen suits and qui tam actions distribute enforcement beyond executive prosecutors. The excerpt reports lower-court acceptance of False Claims Act arrangements and notes that Vermont Agency of Natural Resources v. Stevens reserved the Article II question while addressing standing. Federal programs also depend on state and local implementation and on statutory incentives for cooperation, subject to constitutional limits. These mechanisms make administrative implementation more plural than a single chain of command.

The discussion of privatization draws on Congressional Research Service accounts and Paul Light’s workforce research. Contracting, grants, vouchers, and hybrid entities may offer flexibility and efficiency while reducing the direct application of public-law accountability mechanisms. Management shifts toward supervising contracts and service providers. The reading contrasts public-law commitments to responsibility and rights with New Public Management’s emphasis on performance and autonomy, attributing the competing evaluations to their proponents. It does not resolve every private actor’s legal status or suggest that all contracting escapes law.
